title: U.S. and Iran Near 60-Day Hormuz Deal Tying Sanctions Relief to Nuclear Pledges, Says Axios
teaser: A draft US-Iran deal could reopen the Strait of Hormuz for 60 days, linking sanctions relief to Iran's nuclear pledges.
summary: Axios reported a draft MOU between the U.S. and Iran that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz for 60 days and provide Iran with limited sanctions relief to sell oil. This framework operates on a 'relief for performance' principle: sanctions relief and lifting the U.S. blockade will only happen after Tehran demonstrates compliance. Key terms include Iran clearing mines and agreeing to negotiate the suspension of its uranium enrichment program. The deal also requires the end of the war between Israel and Hezbollah in Lebanon. This diplomatic effort, supported by regional allies like the UAE and Saudi Arabia, centers Iran's nuclear posture and suggests a significant potential de-escalation in the Middle East.
author: Johnathan Wall
content: A draft deal between the United States and Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz toll-free for 60 days, give Tehran limited sanctions relief to sell oil freely, and launch parallel nuclear negotiations - with an announcement possible as early as Sunday, Axios reported Saturday. The framework is built around a principle one U.S. official called "relief for performance." Under the draft memorandum of understanding, Iran clears the mines it deployed in the Strait and the U.S. lifts its blockade on Iranian ports. Broader sanctions relief and the unfreezing of Iranian funds come only after Tehran demonstrates it is delivering - not before. @TheKobeissiLetter outlined the expected terms Saturday, listing the 60-day ceasefire window, Hormuz reopening, free Iranian oil sales, and partial U.S. sanctions relief as the core components of the emerging framework. Iran's nuclear posture sits at the center of it all. Tehran has committed verbally to never pursue nuclear weapons and agreed to negotiate, during the 60-day window, both the suspension of its uranium enrichment program and the removal of its stockpile of highly enriched uranium. The MOU can be extended by mutual consent once the period expires. U.S. forces mobilized in the region in recent months would stay in place throughout. Trump spent Saturday working the phones. He held a conference call with the leaders of the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Egypt, Turkey, and Pakistan - all of whom voiced support for the deal. Field Marshal Asim Munir of Pakistan had spent Friday and Saturday in Tehran as the primary mediator, making Islamabad's hands-on role in brokering the framework impossible to miss. One clause, however, immediately complicated the picture. The draft MOU states that the war between Israel and Hezbollah in Lebanon would end - a condition Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu raised directly with Trump on Saturday, expressing concern. A U.S. official was direct about the tension: "Bibi has his domestic considerations, but Trump has the interests of the U.S. and the global economy to think about." The same official offered a pointed read on the Hezbollah provision. "If Hezbollah behaves, Israel will behave." That framing positions Netanyahu's objections as manageable rather than fatal, though the clause remains live. Trump himself has been pulled between ordering strikes against Iran and pursuing diplomacy, and as of Saturday evening was leaning toward the diplomatic path. Whether Iran's leadership is prepared to follow through is the harder question. The terms had not been finalized as of Saturday evening. title: Meta Settles Kentucky School District Bellwether Case
teaser: Meta settled its Kentucky school-district lawsuit, but the outcome only covers Breathitt County, leaving 1,200 more districts fighting the platform's alleged design-induced costs.
summary:
Meta has settled its bellwether lawsuit with Breathitt County School District in Kentucky. This settlement is notable as it concludes the first test case in a vast, ongoing multidistrict litigation involving roughly 1,200 other school districts. Plaintiffs alleged that platforms' designs, such as 'infinite scroll,' promoted compulsive use, thereby creating measurable school costs for counseling and support.

While Meta's agreement concludes this specific trial track, it does not resolve the larger fight. The central dispute remains whether alleged platform design choices can be proven to cause recoverable expenses for districts. The case generated pressure on all major platforms, which had already settled with the district. Legal representatives emphasized that the focus remains on pursuing justice for the remaining districts, suggesting the systemic legal challenge persists.
author: Markus Kasanmascheff
content: TL;DR Settlement Scope: Meta has settled the Kentucky bellwether suit, but the deal covers only Breathitt County. Trial Timing: The case had been headed to trial next month in federal court in Oakland. Case Pipeline: More than 1,200 related district cases remain pending in the wider social media litigation. Liability Test: Future trials may still test whether alleged platform design choices created reimbursable school costs. Meta Platforms has settled the Kentucky school-district lawsuit on Thursday, becoming the last major platform to resolve the case just before it was set to go to trial next month in federal court in Oakland, California. The Kentucky case was part of a larger federal multidistrict litigation accusing major social media companies of designing platforms that allegedly encouraged compulsive use among students and increased pressure on schools. Breathitt County was chosen as an early bellwether, meaning its claims were set to serve as a test case for how similar school-district lawsuits might play before a jury. Its settlement ends that trial track, but it does not resolve the broader litigation involving roughly 1,200 other school districts. TikTok, Snap, and YouTube had already settled the same case before Meta reached its agreement. That sequence closed the first school-district bellwether, or test case chosen from a larger lawsuit pool, but not the wider multidistrict litigation. Breathitt County was selected as a bellwether, and the settlement applies only to that Kentucky district even though a much larger docket still remains pending. That bellwether role made the case a test of how evidence and legal arguments may play before juries in similar suits. Meta has tied its response to Teen Accounts and other teen-safety protections after the settlement, a position a Meta spokesperson repeated after the case ended. That company stance did not include public settlement terms, leaving the agreement as a case-ending result rather than a public answer to the broader design-liability fight. Why the First Bellwether Ended but the MDL Did Not Breathitt County sought more than $60 million over alleged student harms tied to social media use. That damages request also included a 15-year program aimed at mental-health and learning issues it linked to those harms. Plaintiffs also pointed to infinite scroll as one design feature that kept the dispute focused on product mechanics rather than one isolated moderation decision. Related cases involving the remaining 1,200 school districts are still pending, and the broader litigation has continued to generate pressure on Meta beyond a single Kentucky settlement. Plaintiffs argue that social platforms did more than harm minors: they also pushed schools into counseling, discipline, and learning-support costs that defendants should reimburse. Schools have found they need enhanced mental health counseling resources and rapid changes to student-support practices. Those staffing demands have turned the litigation into a dispute over budgets as well as product design. Attorneys for the school districts cast the Kentucky settlement as only one stop in a much larger fight. "Our focus remains on pursuing justice for the remaining 1,200 school districts who have filed cases." Plaintiffs' attorneys, Attorneys for the school districts (via Courthouse News Service ) Later district suits can still force courts to weigh whether alleged platform-design choices created school costs that can be recovered. That unresolved theory means one settlement closes the first test case, but not the public scrutiny facing the rest of the docket. How the Case Reached a Trial Track Summary-judgment motions filed in September 2025 against Breathitt County and five other school-district plaintiffs helped define the legal questions for the first trial group. That procedural stage pushed the larger fight past pleadings and into arguments over what evidence and damages theories could reach a jury. In 2025, the federal judge overseeing the multidistrict litigation, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, had selected six school districts for the first bellwether track. That selection turned the Kentucky case into an early test of whether juries would accept arguments centered on platform design and district spending. As of October 1, 2025, the Northern California MDL covered more than 2,000 lawsuits , including cases from minors, parents, local governments, and public school districts. That scale means closing the Kentucky settlement lane does not materially shrink the litigation pool or remove the possibility of later district trials. Meta and Google had already taken the first addiction bellwether to a jury stage before the final settlement. That earlier posture explains why resolving the case before trial mattered: a public verdict could have shaped settlement leverage, evidence fights, and damages arguments across the remaining school-district claims. What Plaintiffs Allege and How Meta Responded Plaintiffs say clustered timing of notifications and endless scrolling feeds were built to keep young users on the platforms. Those design allegations are tied to downstream costs for counseling, discipline, and student support rather than to a single moderation dispute. No school-district ruling had found, when Meta settled, that those alleged features created recoverable school costs. Future district cases would still need to show not only that platform features encouraged compulsive use, but also that those design choices can be tied directly to measurable education expenses. Meta's response centers on Teen Accounts and the broader youth-safety defense it has used during the wider addiction litigation. That defense will face a harder legal test if later cases turn school spending records and platform-design evidence into trial exhibits.

title: Meta Tests Forum-App to Turn Facebook Groups Into a Reddit Rival
teaser: Meta launched 'Forum,' an AI-powered app built around Facebook Groups, transforming community posts into a dedicated, Reddit-style Q&A experience.
summary: Meta has launched 'Forum,' a standalone app designed to turn existing Facebook Groups into a centralized, Reddit-like forum for deeper discussion. The app allows users to retain their community history and browse content in a dedicated feed, separating it from the main Facebook clutter. Key features include an AI-powered 'Ask' tab, which synthesizes answers from multiple groups, and an admin AI assistant for moderation. Forum is built upon Facebook Groups, tapping into an estimated 1.8 billion monthly users. While the experience is specialized for Q&A and browsing, posts sync back to the main Facebook platform, solidifying Meta's attempt to reorganize and monetize its massive existing community data pool.
author: Markus Kasanmascheff
content: TL;DR Forum Launch: Meta appears to have launched Forum as a standalone iPhone app built around Facebook Groups. How It Works: The app carries over existing groups, surfaces answer-style discussions, and keeps posts synced with Facebook. Why It Matters: Meta is publicly testing whether group knowledge can become a searchable product without losing the community context or regional flexibility. Meta has launched Forum, a new Facebook app built around Facebook Groups, with the iPhone software now publicly visible in Apple's store. Forum is framed as an active test that users can already inspect rather than a carefully staged debut. Forum stays focused on Facebook groups, which means Meta is packaging years of existing discussions into a separate surface instead of trying to launch a new social network from scratch. People who sign in with Facebook carry over their groups, profile, and activity, so the service starts with community history already in place. Meta had already pushed community features into narrower products with Messenger Communities , giving Forum a foundation of posts and recommendations to reorganize rather than rebuild. Users also have the option to post with a nickname. Forum keeps group conversations in a separate feed instead of mixing them with friends, Pages, and recommended posts in Facebook's main app. Separating the feed gives Meta a clearer way to foreground questions, recommendations, and support threads that would otherwise stay buried in the main feed. That structure also changes the app's starting problem. New discussion apps usually need users to create fresh posts before anyone has a reason to browse them, but Forum arrives with existing groups, old conversations, and account history already attached. Nickname posting adds some distance from a user's real-name Facebook identity while still keeping the service tied to the same community graph. How Forum Repackages Facebook Groups Forum's Ask feature pulls together answers from across groups for opinions, advice, and recommendations. Another description centers responses from Facebook Groups, suggesting that Forum works more like an answer layer built on old posts than a blank space for fresh threads. Posts also sync back to the main Facebook app, so Meta is not fully separating Forum from the larger Facebook ecosystem. Shared syncing keeps the same material moving across both surfaces. That choice also puts Forum closer to Reddit Answers than to a brand-new social network. Meta's AI search engine had already pointed toward searchable recommendations, while the standalone Meta AI app showed the company was still willing to pull useful features out of its main surfaces. Forum now combines both ideas in one product: existing community posts plus a dedicated interface for browsing and answers. Facebook Groups also give Meta a practical advantage over any cold-start rival. Those communities already contain local tips, hobby expertise, support threads, and recommendation chains, so Forum can compete on organization, search, and browsing instead of first having to seed an empty network with new posts. Reddit remains the obvious comparison, but Quora Spaces, Geneva, and Nextdoor also show that specialized discussion products can justify a separate surface when browsing and question-following matter more than a general social feed. Forum's difference is that Meta does not need to import users one by one from the open web, because Facebook Groups already supply the audience, the posts, and much of the recommendation material. What the Public Test Must Prove Meta tests lots of new products publicly, which keeps this rollout explicitly provisional. Forum's admin AI assistant on Forum is designed to help manage groups, moderate content, and keep communities healthy. AI moderation could matter if Meta wants large communities to work smoothly inside a separate app. Forum also appeared without a formal launch event, and some features may vary by country or region. Regional limits leave Meta testing whether people want a dedicated Groups surface that is easier to search and browse than Facebook itself. History gives the experiment more weight. Meta previously ran a dedicated Facebook Groups app before shutting it down in 2017. In October 2024, Meta said Facebook Groups had almost 1.8 billion monthly users , underscoring how much discussion material Forum could tap if the product expands. Meta was also testing a customizable Group AI in that same 2024 push, with answers linked back to relevant posts. Another expansion beyond the iPhone listing, especially if regional limits stay narrow, would show how confident Meta is in turning Facebook Groups into a dedicated answer-and-browsing product.

title: Google Wallet Redesign Brings Cross-Device Pay Verification
teaser: Google Wallet just revolutionized payments: shoppers can now approve purchases on a desktop simply by tapping their Android phone's NFC.
summary:
Google has rolled out a comprehensive redesign of Google Wallet across Android, significantly enhancing payments, identity management, and the user experience. Key features include Cross-device Payment Verification, which allows desktop shoppers to approve purchases via a simple NFC tap and biometric unlock, replacing the need for one-time passcodes. Identity verification is also expanded, with partners like Uber and Intuit using Wallet to selectively share attributes (like age) without handing over full documents. The new UI features dynamic quick access to favorite cards and passes, with dedicated sections for live updates (e.g., flights).
For retailers, Google introduced contactless loyalty enrollment and previewed a digital receipts API to deliver receipts directly within Wallet. The redesign and feature set signal a major push into the competitive digital wallet space.
author: Markus Kasanmascheff
content: TL;DR Redesign Launch: Google has finished the Android-wide Wallet redesign and is rolling it out in phases to every Wallet user. Desktop Checkout: Cross-device Payment Verification lets desktop shoppers approve purchases by tapping an Android phone with NFC and biometric unlock instead of typing a one-time passcode. Identity Expansion: Uber and Intuit's TurboTax are now using Wallet digital ID verification, letting users share attributes such as age without handing over a full document. Retailer Tools: Google added contactless loyalty enrollment and previewed a planned digital receipts API that would deliver receipts inside Wallet. Rollout Window: A consumer-desktop launch date for Cross-device Payment Verification remains unspecified as other I/O 2026 announcements continue this week. Google announced at I/O 2026 that it has finished an Android-wide Wallet redesign and is rolling out Cross-device Payment Verification, a new Google Pay flow that lets desktop shoppers approve purchases by tapping their Android phone instead of typing a one-time passcode. A phased Android rollout puts the new look in front of every Wallet user. Cross-device Payment Verification anchors a broader update that also expands Wallet digital ID verification to Uber and Intuit's TurboTax, adds contactless loyalty enrollment, and previews a digital receipts API for retailers. It builds on the 2022 Wallet relaunch that folded payments and passes into a single Android app and last year's shift away from PayPal , the last major platform change before this one. What The Redesign Changes On the redesigned Wallet homepage, Google offers dynamic quick access to favorites, surfacing the cards or passes a user reaches for often. Boarding passes and other time-sensitive content sit in a fresh layout that pulls flight and ticket details forward when they matter, so a gate change or a sports ticket appears with the relevant context already visible. A "View more" floating action button, or FAB overlay, opens a customizable menu containing the rest of a user's cards, IDs, and saved items. It replaces the older list view that buried less-used entries behind extra taps. Google also surfaces Live Updates for flights and event tickets inside Wallet, keeping gate, time, and venue details current as they change. Each pass is associated with a distinct color that makes it easy to recognize at a glance, part of the colorful new passes UI where that color is now everywhere across the interface. Near-final colorful layouts had appeared in Wallet by May 8, 2026, with pre-launch sightings dating to late March, well ahead of the public I/O 2026 reveal. Cross-Device Verification And Digital ID Cross-device Payment Verification is the standout addition for shoppers. Google Pay positions it as an alternative to one-time passwords for verifying desktop purchases, replacing the SMS code or authenticator prompt that typically gates checkout. A desktop checkout would prompt a shopper to tap an Android phone with NFC and biometric veri f ication , confirming with the same fingerprint or face unlock used to approve in-store taps. Verification arrives alongside Google's Universal Cart for AI-powered online shopping, part of Google's broader I/O 2026 payments groundwork. On the identity side, Uber and Intuit are now using Wallet digital ID verification inside their apps, letting Wallet selectively share attributes such as age or identity without handing over a full document. Selective sharing builds on Wallet's 2024 passport beta and on the Digital Credential API Chrome added for identity sharing, plus Chrome's expanded autofill for passports and licenses . Developer APIs, Competitive Context, And What's Next For developers, Google paired the consumer changes with two retailer-facing additions. Contactless loyalty enrollment lets shoppers add a loyalty card by tapping their phone at a checkout terminal and accepting a notification, skipping the sign-up form, the email opt-in, and the printed card hand-off at the register. Google also previewed a planned digital receipts API that would let retailers deliver receipts directly inside Wallet, alongside the boarding passes and tickets already stored there. A planned Wallet receipts API would let retailers keep customers informed after a purchase and cut down on the support requests that typically follow a sale, though a launch date and the initial launch partners remain unspecified. Wallet's update keeps pace with the broader consumer-wallet field. Samsung Wallet continues shipping on Galaxy devices, Shopify's Shop Pay remains live on retailer checkouts, and Apple Pay remains Google's closest direct rival on the iOS side. With the redesign complete, the sharpest near-term checkpoint is the consumer-desktop rollout window for Cross-device Payment Verification, which remains undated even as the rest of Google's I/O 2026 announcements continue rolling out through the week.

title: OpenAI Puts ChatGPT Inside PowerPoint with New Add-In
teaser: OpenAI just put ChatGPT inside PowerPoint, creating a three-way AI battle royale with Copilot and Claude in the same app.
summary: OpenAI launched a beta ChatGPT add-in for Microsoft PowerPoint, allowing users to build and edit presentations directly within the app. This capability lets users create decks from prompts, uploaded files, or connected accounts like Gmail, Outlook, and SharePoint. The add-in is available to all free and paid ChatGPT tiers. This integration places ChatGPT in fierce competition with Microsoft Copilot and Anthropic Claude within the PowerPoint app. The rollout is underpinned by a non-exclusive 2032 license from OpenAI’s restructured deal with Microsoft, enabling third-party AI distribution. While the add-in offers significant functionality, OpenAI warns of limitations, such as complex template or chart handling, during the beta period.
author: Markus Kasanmascheff
content: TL;DR Beta Launch: OpenAI has launched a ChatGPT add-in for Microsoft PowerPoint in beta for all free and paid ChatGPT tiers. Capability: The sidebar builds and edits decks from prompts, files, or connected Gmail, Outlook, and SharePoint accounts. Beta Limits: OpenAI cautions that complex template, font, and chart handling may not yet be fully supported. Competitive Stake: ChatGPT now sits alongside Microsoft Copilot and Anthropic Claude inside the same PowerPoint app. Legal Mechanism: A non-exclusive 2032 license from the restructured Microsoft-OpenAI deal lets a third-party AI ship directly to Microsoft customers. OpenAI has launched a beta ChatGPT add-in for Microsoft PowerPoint, 2026, putting its chatbot inside the app as a sidebar that builds and edits slides for free and paid ChatGPT users alike. OpenAI's official ChatGPT account on X said the add-in lets users "create and edit presentations directly in PowerPoint" while keeping slides editable inside the app. Free and paid users on Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, Edu, and K-12 ChatGPT tiers all get the beta, the broadest paid Microsoft surface yet for OpenAI's chatbot. Microsoft customers, by contrast, mostly pay nothing for AI inside the app: fewer than 4.5 percent of 450 million Microsoft 365 customers currently pay for Microsoft's own Copilot features . What the Add-In Does Inside PowerPoint, the add-in builds a deck from a prompt or from uploaded notes, documents, spreadsheets, or images. For decks already in progress, ChatGPT can modify or insert slides without starting over, and it can apply reasoning to a finished presentation to surface weak points in the narrative and likely audience objections. ChatGPT can also pull from Gmail, Outlook, and SharePoint when a user connects those accounts, so a deck can draw on existing material in the user's workspace. To install, PowerPoint users open Home, choose Add-ins, search for ChatGPT, and sign in with an OpenAI account; the add-in is also listed in the Microsoft Marketplace . Tier eligibility spans Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, Edu, and K-12, so admin entitlements rather than subscription tier set the gate for many organizations. Reusable Skills playbooks and connected third-party apps inherit the same admin controls, which keeps the rollout consistent across enterprise estates. OpenAI's own FAQ flags template-adherence gaps and partial support for advanced chart, shape, formatting, and slide-management edits during the beta. OpenAI cautions that some advanced PowerPoint capabilities may not be supported yet, including complex template and font handling, and tells users to review the add-in's changes before accepting them, a reminder that the assistant can rewrite or restructure slides in ways that may not match a corporate template. For Business, Enterprise, and Edu tiers, inputs to ChatGPT are not used to improve OpenAI's models by default; consumer tiers can opt out manually. Where ChatGPT Lands in Microsoft's AI Race The ChatGPT Powerpoint add-in arrives in slide-building months behind its closest rivals. Anthropic shipped Claude's slide-building functionality in September 2025 and now operates inside the same Microsoft app. Google has handled the same space through Gemini's tie-in with Slides , and Microsoft's own Copilot already runs inside PowerPoint as the first-party AI panel, with an agent mode added this February . Three AI options now share one application: Copilot from Microsoft, Claude from Anthropic, and ChatGPT from OpenAI, each tied to a different account and pricing model. For many paid PowerPoint users, ChatGPT is the first non-Copilot option that does not require a separate desktop or web tool. The restructured Microsoft-OpenAI partnership is what lets a third-party AI sit inside Microsoft's app at all. Microsoft no longer holds exclusive sales rights to OpenAI's models, and the revised deal gives Microsoft a 27 percent equity stake plus a non-exclusive license through 2032 to OpenAI's intellectual property. OpenAI in return can distribute its products through other cloud providers, and that non-exclusive license is the legal mechanism letting OpenAI ship ChatGPT directly to Microsoft customers without going through Copilot. UBS analyst Karl Keirstead framed the competitive squeeze in plain terms. "Microsoft, and frankly all the software firms, are facing something they haven't faced in 10-plus years, which is extraordinarily innovative new rivals. And expecting any large incumbent like Microsoft to pivot as fast as OpenAI and Anthropic are able to is probably too demanding." Karl Keirstead, UBS analyst (via Fortune ) Two next signals will measure how far the non-exclusive 2032 license carries ChatGPT inside Microsoft's apps: general availability for the PowerPoint add-in beyond beta, and a comparable ChatGPT integration for Microsoft Word, which OpenAI has not yet announced. Either step would put ChatGPT alongside Microsoft's own Copilot in a second Office surface and test whether the partnership keeps opening Office to a third-party assistant.

title: Trump says Iran negotiations proceeding in 'orderly and constructive manner;' warns against rushing
teaser: Trump affirms Iran talks are moving cautiously, warning against rushing a deal that must dismantle Iran's nuclear sites and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
summary: Donald Trump reported that talks with Iran regarding the end of hostilities and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz are progressing 'in an orderly and constructive manner.' He cautioned, however, that negotiators must not rush, asserting that 'time is on our side.' The proposed comprehensive deal would end the conflict, unfreeze Iranian assets, and curb Tehran's nuclear program. Netanyahu reinforced these demands, insisting any agreement must include dismantling Iran's nuclear enrichment sites. Furthermore, the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports remains until a finalized agreement is signed, while Israel maintained its security concerns regarding Lebanon remain a sticking point.
content: US President Donald Trump holds an umbrella as he steps off of Air Force One upon arrival at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on May 22, 2026. Trump said that "time is on our side" in the push to end the nearly three-month-old conflict that has whipsawed global energy markets and spiked gasoline prices in the U.S. "The negotiations are proceeding in an orderly and constructive manner, and I have informed my representatives not to rush into a deal in that time is on our side," Trump said in the social media post. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a social media post on Sunday that he spoke to Trump on Saturday night about the "memorandum of understanding to reopen the Straits of Hormuz and the upcoming negotiations toward a final agreement on Iran's nuclear program." The Israeli leader said that any deal with Iran must include limiting its nuclear capabilities, which Netanyahu said means "dismantling Iran's nuclear enrichment sites and removing its enriched nuclear material from its territory." He also said that Trump "reaffirmed Israel's right to defend itself against threats on every front, including Lebanon." Israeli strikes in Lebanon have been a sticking point in past negotiations between the U.S. and Iran. This story is developing. Please check back for updates.

title: Google’s AI Search Shift Towards Agents Gives Rivals a Clearer Pitch
teaser: Google's AI search is dominant, but a bug means searching 'disregard' triggers a chat reply instead of a definition.
summary: Google is intensely integrating AI into Search, positioning AI Overviews as a core, assistant-like feature across desktop and mobile. While Google remains dominant (90.01% global share), this trend forces rivals to clearly differentiate: Microsoft Bing is also adopting an AI-forward approach. Smaller competitors, like Kagi and Startpage, are countering by selling privacy, ad-free models, or independent indexing, emphasizing user control. However, Google's rapid push into AI is facing immediate challenges; recently, a bug has emerged where the AI Overviews misinterprets single-word action queries such as 'disregard' or 'ignore' as commands, replacing the intended dictionary definition with a free-form, chat-style AI reply.
author: Markus Kasanmascheff
content: TL;DR Search Shift: Google has pushed Search further into AI-driven responses, but Bing's Copilot Search shows that the largest mainstream rival is also moving toward AI summaries rather than away from them. Alternative Models: Kagi sells ad-free paid search, while Startpage, DuckDuckGo, Qwant, Brave, Ecosia, and Mojeek emphasize privacy, independent indexing, or more visible control over AI features. Market Reality: Google still held 90.01% of global search traffic in March 2026, so the opening for rivals is clearer differentiation across AI-heavy, privacy-first, paid, regional, and independent search models. Google announced substantial changes to Search at I/O 2026 and pushed it further into conversational AI, giving privacy-focused and lower-AI rivals a clearer reason to exist. An earlier redesign had already pulled AI Mode closer to the default experience. Elizabeth Reid, the leader of the Search organization at Google, framed the redesign as the product's biggest upgrade in more than 25 years. According to Google, AI Mode has already surpassed 1 billion monthly users , so the main search box now sits at the center of a mass-market product rather than a side experiment. Google has folded follow-up questions in AI Overviews into the same product path after Google launched follow-up question support in January. Google still handled 90.01% of worldwide search traffic in March 2026, while the DOJ's appeal in Google's antitrust search-monopoly case kept pressure on how the company shapes Search. That scale leaves only limited room for classic search rivals, but it does not make the competitive landscape simple. Microsoft Bing remains the most important large-scale alternative to Google, and its direction matters precisely because it is not a low-AI or privacy-first retreat from Google's model. Copilot Search in Bing uses summarized answers, cited sources, and follow-up discovery, putting Microsoft's product on the AI-forward side of the market. The split is therefore sharper than Google versus every other search engine. Google and Bing are pushing mainstream search toward AI-assisted answers, while smaller rivals can sell a different bargain: fewer ads, less tracking, more visible links, independent indexes, or more control over when AI appears. The New Search Experience Makes Control a Selling Point Google's answer boxes now keep follow-up questions inside the result, and AI Overviews plus AI Mode now form a single AI search experience across desktop and mobile. Google's first search agents can monitor topics, tasks, or projects for users, pushing the product further from a plain list of links and closer to an assistant. In 2024, Google had already added a web-only filter for people who wanted direct results. For smaller rivals, the pitch is simpler: the largest search products are building experiences that keep users inside AI-driven exchanges for longer, while alternative engines can promise less AI, more privacy, more curation, or more user control. What Kagi, Startpage, and Qwant Offer Kagi is making the clearest paid pitch. Its search product promises no ads, no tracking, which means the service is funded by subscribers instead of advertising. For users who dislike the ad-and-AI bundle shaping mainstream search, that is a direct alternative rather than a vague privacy slogan. Kagi's trade-off is price. Kagi pricing starts at $5 a month for 300 searches and rises to $10 a month for unlimited use. It also lets users refine results with lenses, including narrower filters for jobs like academic research, so the product is selling curation as much as raw search access. Startpage takes the privacy route instead. Its IP address removal and unprofiled results keep the search habit familiar while reducing how much identity travels with the request. That approach gives users a more familiar search page while cutting down on the personal data that travels with each query. Its Anonymous View proxy lets people access and explore entire websites privately. Startpage also offers a standard search experience out of the box, without much AI by default, which gives it a simpler pitch for people who want fewer AI layers in the results page itself. Qwant belongs in the same privacy-first conversation, but with a more explicit European angle. The search engine says it does not retain search data, does not sell personal data, and is hosted in Europe. That makes its pitch less about beating Google at scale and more about offering a familiar search surface with stronger privacy and data-sovereignty claims. The Wider Market Splits Between Scale, Privacy, and Index Independence DuckDuckGo sits closer to the mass market, but it is also making the control pitch more explicit. Users can Disable Duck.ai. DuckDuckGo had already framed privacy as a differentiator in its earlier privacy-first AI search launch . In practice, that makes it an easier recommendation for users who want AI to stay optional instead of becoming the first layer of search. Brave and Ecosia are working the same opening from different angles. Brave keeps optional AI features at the edge of the experience, while Ecosia lets users disable them at any time from Ecosia's settings even though an AI chat entry point still stays visible. Both are effectively betting that user control can matter more than maximum AI automation. Mojeek adds a different kind of distinction. It is much smaller than Google, Bing, or DuckDuckGo, but it emphasizes that its web results come from its own crawler and index rather than from a Google or Bing syndication layer. That makes it relevant for users who are not just looking for privacy controls, but for a search provider with a more independent view of the web. Scale and regional search also complicate the picture. Yahoo remains part of the search-share conversation, while Yandex, Baidu, and Naver matter in markets where language, local services, regulation, and default placement shape user behavior differently. They are not all privacy alternatives, and they do not all compete for the same users, but they show why global search competition is broader than the privacy-focused engines most visible to U.S. and European users. AI Answer Engines Create a Different Kind of Pressure AI-native answer engines complicate the market from the opposite direction. Perplexity and ChatGPT Search are not traditional search engines in the old list-of-links sense, but they compete for many of the same informational queries that once started on Google. That creates an unusual opening. Some users may leave Google's default experience because they want fewer AI layers and more visible web results. Others may skip classic search because they want more direct AI answers with source links. Google's redesign is a response to both pressures, and it makes the search market less about one replacement for Google and more about several competing models for finding information. DuckDuckGo at 1.84% of U.S. search share shows how small the challengers remain next to Google. If privacy tools, paid ad-free search, independent indexes, regional search ecosystems, and optional AI controls can move even niche share upward, Google's redesign will have turned dissatisfaction with AI-heavy defaults into a measurable opening for rivals.

title: In all of human history, has there ever been a commodity with infinite demand, as there appears to be for intelligence?...
teaser: Intelligence is treated as a commodity with unprecedented and potentially infinite demand, leading to a continuously shifting demand curve in the modern economy.
summary: Chris Anderson posits that intelligence represents a commodity with unprecedented and potentially infinite demand, suggesting it is the fundamental demand driver in the modern economy. As intelligence becomes cheaper and more accessible, it opens up entirely new applications and markets, ensuring that the demand growth rate is the more critical metric than reaching a simple equilibrium.
author: Chris Anderson
content:
In all of human history, has there ever been a commodity with infinite demand, as there appears to be for intelligence? I can't think of one. Even compute, energy or just silicon/sand are just downstream of intelligence, which is the main demand driver.

In economics, rather than modeling the usual price/demand curve to reach an equilibrium, perhaps you'd have to model price/*rate of demand growth* (ie, the derivative of demand, or some other indicator of velocity)

But the end result is the same -- the demand curve keeps moving to the right, maybe forever. 

Which I think is unprecedented.

title: Google Asks D.C. Circuit to Overturn Search Monopoly Ruling
teaser: Google appeals a search monopoly ruling, arguing rivals are picking its services for quality, not due to anti-competitive lock-in.
summary: Google has appealed a federal antitrust ruling that found the company illegally maintained a search monopoly through default agreements with device makers like Apple. Google argues the ruling incorrectly conflated harm to competitors with harm to the competitive process itself. The original judgment required Google to share vast amounts of data (search index, user data) with rivals, including generative AI companies like OpenAI. Google's appeal also contends that Apple chose Google's engine due to its high quality, not exclusionary practices. Meanwhile, the Justice Department and state attorneys general have filed a cross-appeal, demanding stronger remedies, including the divestiture of Chrome, which the trial judge initially declined to impose.
author: Markus Kasanmascheff
content: TL;DR Appeal Filed: Google has asked the D.C. Circuit to overturn Judge Mehta's search-monopoly ruling and his September 2025 remedies order. Legal Argument: Google says the trial court confused harm to competitors with harm to competition and that Apple chose its engine on quality. Remedies at Stake: The order would force Google to share its search index, user data, and ad-syndication services with rivals, including OpenAI. Cross-Appeal: The Justice Department and state attorneys general are separately seeking stronger relief, including the Chrome divestiture Mehta declined to impose. Google's 111-page appeal brief reached the D.C. Circuit on the 22nd of May, contesting both Judge Amit Mehta's August 2024 liability ruling and his September 2025 remedies order . Inside, Google tells the court that "Google just prevailed in the marketplace fair and square." Both rulings are now under appeal. In August 2024, he found that Google illegally maintained a monopoly in U.S. general search through exclusive default-search agreements with Apple, Samsung, and other Android device makers. His September 2, 2025 order then required Google to share its search index, user-interaction data, and certain ad-syndication services with qualifying competitors, including generative AI rivals such as OpenAI. Justice Department and state attorneys-general lawyers have also noticed a cross-appeal seeking stronger structural relief, including a Chrome divestiture the trial judge declined to impose. Inside the Brief: Merit, Not Monopolization Google's affirmative case rests on Section 2 of the Sherman Act, the federal antitrust provision against monopolizing conduct. Google urges the D.C. Circuit to overturn the search-monopoly remedies, calling Mehta's liability finding "as basic an error of antitrust law as a court can make," arguing the trial court conflated harm to competitors with harm to the competitive process itself. Google says it already handled about 80% of U.S. search queries by 2009, well before any conduct challenged in the case. On the Apple-default arrangement that anchored the trial court's 2024 liability finding, Google argues Apple picked it as the highest-quality option, not as a product of exclusionary lock-in. Apple receives roughly $20 billion a year for the default placement Google now appeals on Safari, iPhones, iPads, and Macs. Mehta's decision treated that payment as a central factual basis of the liability finding. Distribution partners were free to choose rivals, Google's brief contends, and no trial finding established that customers would have switched absent the challenged agreements. Google's brief frames its central legal theory for the appellate court directly: "At bottom, the district court's failure to heed the elemental distinction in antitrust law between conduct that harms competitors and conduct that harms the competitive process produced exactly the result that the law is designed to prevent. This is truly the case of a successful competitor being turned upon because it has won." Google appeal brief Remedies the Appeal Wants Vacated On the remedies front, Google argues that Judge Mehta "egregiously exceeded" his discretion when he ordered the data-sharing regime. His September 2025 order spared Google from a forced Chrome sale and from any Android divestiture. Mehta still required the company to hand qualifying competitors slices of its search index, user-interaction data, and certain search and text ad-syndication services. Google's brief calls those data-transfer and syndication requirements an extraordinary judicial step that would manufacture artificial competition rather than reward firms that built their own. AI rivals draw the sharpest objection in the filing. Google's brief says those generative AI competitors "did not even exist" during the conduct period now under appellate review, and contends those rivals are already growing rapidly without needing access to Google's assets. OpenAI's previously expressed interest in Chrome underscored, in Google's framing, how the data-sharing regime would route search assets to AI rivals that postdate the conduct at issue. Lee-Anne Mulholland, Google vice president of regulatory affairs, paired the brief with a corporate statement Google issued the same day. "We are asking the court to overturn this flawed decision - partners and users have many options and choose Google because it provides the best, most helpful results." Lee-Anne Mulholland, Google vice president of regulatory affairs What Comes Next A structural counterweight is already in motion at the same court. Justice Department lawyers and a coalition of state attorneys general formally noticed their cross-appeal of Judge Mehta's remedies order in February 2026, arguing the trial court did not go far enough and preserving their request for the forced Chrome divestiture Mehta declined to impose. Captioned United States and Plaintiff States v. Google LLC , the underlying case was filed in October 2020 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia by the Antitrust Division and a state-attorneys-general coalition. Before the September 2025 data-sharing remedy can take effect against Google's search index, user-interaction data, and ad-syndication services, the D.C. Circuit must rule on Google's appeal and the DOJ-state cross-appeal.

title: No captain, my captain: Navantia floats crewless warship
teaser: Navantia unveils the LASV75, a 75m, uncrewed 'drone' warship meant to redefine naval power and safeguard the UK's undersea infrastructure.
summary: Navantia has unveiled the Large Autonomous Surface Vessel (LASV75), a concept for a sophisticated, uncrewed warship designed to form the core of a 'hybrid navy.' Measuring 75 meters and displacing about 1,000 tonnes, the LASV75 is modular and entirely uncrewed, featuring no crew spaces but integrating advanced payloads and electric propulsion. Designed to complement vessels like the Type 45 destroyer, its primary roles include supporting the UK's Atlantic Bastion strategy—protecting undersea cables and tracking submarines. Experts note that the uncrewed nature and modular design promise greater operational coverage and cost efficiency compared to traditional crewed warships.
content:
Offbeat No captain, my captain: Navantia floats crewless warship Spanish shipbuilder's 75-meter drone vessel comes with sensors, modular payloads, and no room for sailors Shipbuilder Navantia has put forward a design for an uncrewed
warship intended to complement existing naval vessels in what has been dubbed a
" hybrid navy, " although it may not be an exact fit for any current requirements. Developed by the UK arm of the Spanish firm, the Large
Autonomous Surface Vessel, or LASV75, is basically a large seagoing drone that
is armed like a conventional warship. Two LASV75 uncrewed surface vessels accompanying a Royal Navy Type 45 destroyer at sea Navantia As its name suggests, the LASV75 is 75 meters long, making it
about half as long as one of the Royal Navy's Type 45 destroyers and closer in size to one of the River-class patrol vessels, with a displacement of about 1,000
tonnes. It is designed to be entirely uncrewed, with no bridge or
crew spaces, and adaptable for different missions via a modular design. Promotional
images also show the vessel carrying several shipping containers, which
have become a common way for navies to quickly add extra capabilities to a
vessel. According to Navantia, the design allows for construction of
the drone at pace and scale, and it is expected to cost significantly less than
crewed warships, although the company did not specify exactly how quickly or cheaply it could be built. The modularity extends to both mission payloads and
engineering systems, Navantia told us, allowing the LASV75 to be tailored to
the roles required, from installed power to weapons and sensor capability. A prominent feature is a mast designed to host a number of
sensor configurations, but we were puzzled by the apparent lack of funnels for
engine exhaust. The ship is equipped with Integrated Full Electric Power and
Propulsion (IFEP), Navantia said, meaning it uses diesel generators to drive
electric motors and power everything else aboard. It has waterline
exhausts. The LASV75 was designed to meet the Royal Navy's concept of
a hybrid navy, but also to serve wider demand for autonomous vessels. Its size will
enable it to have the range and endurance for task group operations in the open
ocean, the company claims, so it can undertake escort duties or support the Royal
Navy's Atlantic
Bastion strategy to protect undersea infrastructure around the UK, such as cables and pipelines, and to track Russian submarines. The vessel could potentially meet the requirement for a Type 92 sloop that the Royal Navy outlined for Atlantic Bastion, effectively an uncrewed ship that can patrol the North Atlantic looking out for submarines. This role is currently filled by the Type 23 frigate, and will be taken by the Type 26 when that comes into service, but the expectation
is that a flotilla of uncrewed Type 92 vessels would allow for greater uninterrupted coverage of the ocean. "Autonomous vessels are fundamental to the future of
sovereign defence capabilities. Naval capabilities of the future will comprise
a hybrid mixture of crewed warships with uncrewed escorts and ancillary ships,"
said Derek Jones, Navantia UK chief commercial and business development officer. "At Navantia UK, we're investing heavily
in our four shipyards to turn them into ideal partners to
deliver this vision of the future." The company is currently building the Fleet Solid Support
(FSS) vessels for the Royal Fleet Auxiliary, which will provide supplies to
Royal Navy ships at sea. ®

title: HP investigating BIOS updates that leave premium laptop users in boot loop limbo
teaser: Mandatory BIOS updates are leaving premium HP laptops unbootable, causing elite workstations to fail in 'boot loop limbo'.
summary: HP customers are encountering severe issues with mandatory BIOS updates for premium laptops, leading to devices stuck in 'boot loop limbo' and unbootable states. These critical updates, automatically pushed via Windows Update, have caused problems like BSODs and complete freezing. Affected models and specific broken BIOS versions include ZBook Ultra G1a (versions 01.04.03 and 01.04.05) and EliteBook X G1a (versions 01.03.11 and 01.05.00). While temporary fixes exist, reverting to a stable version is difficult, often requiring specific hardware like an HP USB-C to Ethernet dongle. HP has acknowledged the widespread issues and is investigating. The company recently committed to the open-source LVFS initiative, hoping to improve firmware reliability.
content: Personal Tech HP investigating BIOS updates that leave premium laptop users in boot loop limbo Slowdowns, crashes, BSODs reported on pricey mobile workstations HP customers are reporting problems with BIOS updates for the PC maker's premium laptops. Over the past few months , customers have used forums to register complaints over unbootable devices, spikes in fan noise, and Blue Screens of Death following BIOS firmware updates. An example cropped up in April , when a user of a ZBook Ultra G1a ( a very expensive mobile workstation ) complained that a BIOS update had caused the machine to "freeze completely during the boot process." The customer wasn't alone: other forums including Reddit showed many other users experiencing problems. The cause appears to be a BIOS update, flagged as critical, and pushed through Windows Update. As a critical update, the patch was automatically applied, which is where the fun begins for affected users. In the case of the ZBook Ultra G1a, the broken BIOS versions are 01.04.03 and 01.04.05. The problematic BIOS versions for the EliteBook X G1a are 01.03.11 and 01.05.00. Stopping the update is one option, and the BIOS lets users prevent the operating system from initiating updates. However, once the update has completed, reverting to a known working version is problematic. Users have reported some success using the network BIOS downgrade functionality, but only with an HP USB-C to Ethernet dongle. This is far from HP's first rodeo when it comes to BIOS updates turning laptops into expensive paperweights. In 2024, an update left some devices irretrievably bricked and customers facing hefty hardware repair bills. The current issues come at a time when Microsoft is working to improve the reliability of Windows and applying greater scrutiny to third-party drivers sent through Windows Update . The service can also be used for BIOS and other firmware updates. HP told The Register : "HP is aware of purported BIOS issues and is looking into the matter." The hardware vendor suggested that affected users contact its support teams for assistance. Timing is everything. On May 20, Richard Hughes of the Linux Vendor Firmware Service (LVFS) project announced that HP was joining Lenovo and Dell as premier sponsors. The LVFS initiative is an open source firmware updating solution. Here's hoping that HP is only bringing its dollars and not any of the BIOS update quality problems currently frustrating some of its customers. ®

title: Why Nuro thinks being a robotaxi ‘second mover’ gives it an advantage
teaser: Nuro believes being a 'second mover' in the robotaxi market gives it an edge, using Waymo’s lead to refine its systems before launching a broad service.
summary: Despite Waymo's current leadership in robotaxis, Nuro, a company founded by Google self-driving car veterans, argues that being a 'second mover' provides a unique strategic advantage. Nuro is partnering with Uber and Lucid to deploy its Level 4 autonomous technology in a fleet of Lucid Gravity SUVs, aiming for a broad operational domain on day one. Co-CEO Dave Ferguson argues that observing industry leaders like Waymo's successes and failures allows Nuro to 'sanity check' and reevaluate its system. Nuro plans a highly integrated service involving all three companies, and the model emphasizes transparency and building public trust through evidence of superior safety compared to human drivers. Nuro also plans to license its advanced AI driving system for various applications, beyond robotaxis.
author: Andrew J. Hawkins
content: Waymo is the undisputed leader in the robotaxi space, operating a fleet of over 3,000 driverless cars in at least 10 cities across the US. A number of companies, including Tesla, Zoox, Avride, and Motional, are racing to catch up with the Alphabet-owned firm. But what if being No. 2 was actually better? Nuro, the delivery robot company created by veterans of Google's self-driving car project, thinks it has a decent shot at occupying the slot. After pivoting from delivery to robotaxis in 2024, Nuro struck a deal with Uber and Lucid to deploy tens of thousands of robotaxis all across the US - netting itself hundreds of millions of dollars in investment from Uber in the process. Nuro plans on launching the service in San Francisco later this year. And earlier this month, it was granted the first of several permits it will need in order to launch that service. It's almost better for Nuro that Waymo is scaling at the pace that it is, said Dave Ferguson, cofounder and co-CEO of Nuro. Its early successes, as well as its stumbles and missteps, then become fodder for Nuro's engineers to reassess and reevaluate, with the goal of answering the question: Could we have done better? What if being No. 2 was actually better? "There is a lot of value in this sort of classic second mover perspective," Ferguson said in a recent interview. "We have a huge amount of respect for Waymo ... In some of the rare cases where they're having challenges, [Nuro is] using those to kick the tires on our system and make sure that it would behave in a way that we're comfortable and proud of as well." The fact that Ferguson has respect for Waymo isn't a surprise. He got his start at Google's self-driving car project that would go on to become Waymo, along with Nuro cofounder and co-CEO Jiajun Zhu. The two left Google in 2016 to found Nuro , first as a robot delivery service, and now as an aspiring robotaxi operator. Nuro also aims to license its autonomous driving technology to outside companies, including car companies that want to use it for advanced driver-assist systems and personally owned autonomous vehicles - though it has yet to announce any deals. Nuro cofounder and co-CEO Dave Ferguson. Photo by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge To be sure, Nuro is late to the robotaxi party. While Nuro was handling groceries, Waymo was handling passengers. But Ferguson argues that Nuro's technology is easily transferable to robotaxis - even if its passenger experience is still zero. That's where his "second mover" theory comes into play. Unlike Waymo, which had to discover many operational challenges firsthand, Nuro believes it will benefit from watching the Alphabet-owned company operate a large-scale robotaxi service before fully launching its own. To that end, Ferguson wants Nuro's robotaxi service to be broadly useful when it first launches. He suggested that some features, like freeway driving, may arrive later, but that the launch will not follow an ultra-incremental playbook where the company initially handles only certain scenarios before slowly adding more complex ones over time. That said, Nuro doesn't plan to include "the entire South Bay on day one," Ferguson said. "The plan is very much on day one for this to be a very useful service," he said. "This is not going to be only protected intersections, and then slowly we add unprotected ... It's going to be a very broad [operational design domain] to begin with." The Uber-Lucid-Nuro robotaxi service is unique, insofar as it involves three distinct companies: a rideshare network, an automaker, and an autonomous vehicle startup. Under the arrangement, Nuro develops the sensing and compute stack and works closely with Lucid to integrate that technology into the vehicle, the Lucid Gravity SUV . The integration happens directly on Lucid's production line, meaning the vehicles leave the factory already equipped with Level 4 autonomy. Those completed vehicles are then sold to Uber, which becomes the owner and operator of the fleet. The rideshare company will manage the depots and operational infrastructure associated with running the service. Uber will also manage remote assistance for the vehicles, Ferguson said. Remote assistance has come under fire lately, with some members of Congress demanding Waymo and others be more forthcoming about their use of offsite workers to oversee the vehicles. Ferguson said this has led to the spread of misinformation about companies using remote workers to actively control the robotaxis. What they really do, he said, is answer questions and provide prompts to help the vehicles when they get confused. "The view that the public probably jumps to when they're told remote assistance of self-driving vehicles is someone in a dark room driving a car around like they're playing a video game," he said. "I think that is pretty far from how remote assistance typically works." Nuro's long-term goal is to build the most capable AI driving system possible, with the intention of putting it to work in a variety of ways, including delivery, he said. To that end, Nuro's longevity in the field ensures that the company can apply the lessons from its older, more rules-based machine learning systems, as well as its current end-to-end learning models that produce a more naturalistic driving style. According to Ferguson, that legacy is critical even as the industry transitions toward more AI-heavy approaches. "You can think of this as sanity checking to make sure that what we're doing doesn't get too close to pedestrians, doesn't get too close to other vehicles, isn't violating any traffic rules," he said. He acknowledged that robotaxis are suffering from a lack of public trust, especially around edge cases and other incidents in which autonomous vehicles block traffic. Nuro intends to follow Waymo's model of being transparent with some of its driving statistics in the interest of building trust with its customers, Ferguson said. "The more evidence we have of Nuro and Uber and Lucid providing a product that is dramatically safer and better for our streets than a human-driven vehicle ... the better that is for everyone," he said. The company is still trying to "strike the right balance of how much detail do we provide, such that it's actually understandable and relatable to the general public." But Ferguson said he's confident they'll get there. Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. Andrew J. title: Move over, seltzer. Non-carbonated drinks are taking the spotlight
teaser: Seltzer fatigue is hitting the drink industry: Non-carbonated beverages, spearheaded by brands like Surfside, are taking the spotlight in both alcohol and non-alcoholic sectors.
summary: Consumer beverage preferences are undergoing a major shift, with non-carbonated (still) drinks overtaking flavored seltzers due to 'seltzer fatigue.' This trend is driven largely by Gen Z, who prioritize wellness, digestive comfort, and trying new products. In the alcohol sector, ready-to-drink premixed cocktails—led by brands like Surfside—saw volume grow 46.4% in the last 52 weeks. Surfside, a non-carbonated iced tea, was named the fastest-growing alcohol brand in the U.S. by 2024, suggesting consumer desire for fizz-free options. Non-alcoholic drinks are also adapting, with energy drink brands expanding their lines with fizz-free options to better appeal to consumers who prefer a smoother, non-carbonated flavor profile.
content: Surfside drinks on display at the trade show during CinemaCon 2026 at Caesars Palace in Las Vegas on April 15, 2026. Travis P Ball | AP About a decade ago, sales of LaCroix began to skyrocket. Soon, flavored seltzers were everywhere, from grocery store refrigerators to liquor store shelves. But the era of bubbles looks like it is winding down, thanks to seltzer fatigue. Now, non-carbonated drinks, from Liquid Death to Surfside Iced Teas, are taking the spotlight. "If you think about where there's more growth, where there's more consumer interest relative to a few years ago, it's a shift more to still, across both [alcohol] and non-alc," said Randy Burt, Americas director of consumer products at consulting firm AlixPartners. That's not to say seltzers and other carbonated beverages will disappear. But their growth has slowed, as Generation Z increasingly seeks out options without bubbles and beverage companies focus more of their innovation efforts on fizz-free drinks. Look no further than the alcohol category. Malt-based hard seltzers, which includes White Claw, saw volume drop 1.1% in the 52 weeks ended April 26, compared with the year-ago period, according to data from market research firm Circana . On the other hand, ready-to-drink premixed cocktails saw volume grow 46.4% in the same time, fueled by growth from Surfside, Sun Cruiser, BuzzBallz and Anheuser-Busch InBev's Cutwater Spirits, which has both carbonated and non-carbonated options. Bursting bubbles Much of the driving force behind the switch from bubbly to noncarbonated drinks is coming from Gen Z, which is typically defined as people born between 1997 and 2012. Over their lifetime, soda consumption has dropped dramatically from its peak in 1998, reusable water bottles have become a staple accessory, and a plethora of new drinks like refreshers and dirty soda have gone mainstream. Broadly, Gen Z wants to try new products. While older generations show more brand loyalty to their favorite beer or cocktail, younger consumers have a different mentality. "We're seeing a lot of promiscuity within consumption and alcohol around new products," said Scott Scanlon, executive vice president of alcoholic beverages for Circana , citing the rise of White Claw and Truly about eight years ago. "Now what we're seeing is then consumers jump to the newest product - that's Surfside, Sun Cruiser because of that." He sees a generational shift between Gen Z and their predecessors, millennials, who couldn't get enough of seltzers. As Gen Z reaches drinking age, their alcoholic preferences reflect that generational divide. Non-carbonated alcoholic drinks like Surfside and BeatBox are stealing "share of throat" from hard seltzers, which have seen their growth slow. "Gen Z is a lot more likely to order tea-based beverages at happy hour, and they're sort of moving from carbonated - or seltzers - as their default, 'better for you' pick," Burt said. "I think that's part of the shift, toward wellness and functionality that you're seeing happen, especially from a Gen Z perspective." For fans of some beverages , like functional teas and coffees that target stress relief or immune support, going fizz-free makes more sense, given the drinks' non-carbonated base. Plus, some consumers do not view carbonation as the healthy option. Carbonated water is slightly acidic, which can wear down tooth enamel when consumed in large quantities, especially if the seltzer uses citric acid for flavoring. Plus fizzy drinks can cause bloating and burping for some people . And then there's the association bubbles of any kind can share with sugary sodas. What's the tea? Alcohol is leading the trend, thanks to the meteoric rise of Surfside. Indie vodka distiller Stateside Brands launched the hard iced tea brand in 2022. The ready-to-drink beverage uses vodka as a base and iced tea and lemonade as a mixer. At the time of its launch, carbonation was everywhere across the alcohol industry. "Among the options out there were carbonated iced tea and carbonated lemonade, which is a little less unusual, but we were just like 'What the heck, man? Who carbonates iced tea?' That seems unholy," said Stateside co-founder and CEO Clement Pappas. Consumers seemed to agree. By 2024, Surfside was the fastest-growing alcohol brand in the U.S., based on Nielsen IQ data. "I think there was a huge pent-up demand for non-carbonated options," Pappas said. "There are very few out there, especially in a ready-to-drink format." Surfside's customer base skews female. Pappas said that many of the brand's fans dislike carbonation because they find it leads to bloating, particularly after consuming several drinks in a sitting. Stateside is leaning further into fizz-free beverages with its latest brand: Super Lyte. The brand still uses vodka as a base, but the mixer is inspired by classic sports drinks. While Surfside may have popped the seltzer bubble, other non-carbonated alcoholic drinks have grown quickly since then. Volume growth of Cutwater's canned cocktails has nearly doubled over the last year, according to Scanlon. BeatBox, a wine-based punch brand that is majority owned by InBev, has also seen demand for its drinks skyrocket since the alcohol giant has ramped up its distribution. And then there is BuzzBallz pre-mixed cocktails, which launched in 2009 but has seen its growth rocket after its acquisition by Sazerac in 2024. Established alcohol players have also been trying to take on Surfside, further boosting the profile of non-carbonated drinks in the category. Twisted Tea owner Boston Beer launched Sun Cruiser in 2024 with the aim of directly competing with Surfside. So far, Surfside retains a bigger slice of overall market share, although Sun Cruiser is growing faster these days. Bubble-free Celsius heats up Cases of Celsius energy drinks at a store in San Francisco on March 17, 2025. David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images On the non-alcoholic side, the shift toward bubble-free drinks isn't as strong, according to AlixPartners' Burt. Some carbonated drinks are still showing strong growth; PepsiCo's Poppi, as well as energy drinks like Celsius and Ghost, are seeing strong demand. But there are signs that the soft drink landscape is shifting. Celsius, for example, expanded its fizz-free line of energy drinks earlier this year, inspired by Gen Z's focus on wellness and the general trend toward noncarbonated beverages in other categories. Typically, carbonated options dominate the energy drink aisle, allowing Celsius to stand out and win over customers who might otherwise stick to tea or coffee for their caffeine fix. The brand's pre-existing noncarbonated peach mango green tea flavor is consistently a top 10 performer for Celsius and is currently in the number four slot across all of its flavors, according to Celsius Chief Brand Officer Kyle Watson. The expanded line has helped Celsius grow sales from Gen Z and women, two key segments in the energy drink category. "In focus groups that we've had ... even our brand ambassadors across all of our universities, a lot of them talk about how they don't like drinking sparkling," Watson said. When consumers drink "functional beverages - like those touting high protein content, prebiotics, caffeine or other benefits - they want "a better flavor experience," according to Watson. Watson said that part of the appeal of the fizz-free line is how it goes down "really smooth," making it a better pairing for meals. About 37% of Celsius consumers consume their energy drinks with a meal, according to Watson. And Celsius has made sure to put its noncarbonated bona fides front and center of the line's packaging. "With the expansion, we also wanted to make sure that the callout around being fizz-free and that attribute of it being noncarbonated and having that smooth, refreshing flavor profile was more prevalent on the actual can design," Watson said. Some other beverage brands are betting big on the swing away from fizz. "Our product is extremely drinkable because of the lack of carbonation," Hint CEO Michael Pengue said in an interview. Founded in 2005, the flavored water company has a devoted fan base, particularly in Silicon Valley. But the brand has gotten "dusty," and its growth has stagnated, according to Pengue. He is hoping that consumers' shift away from bubbles will boost sales, along with new packaging and a sexy new ad campaign. (While Hint has some sparkling options, it is a much smaller part of the brand's portfolio, according to Pengue.) Earlier in Pengue's career, he led Nestle's water and tea brands, which includes Perrier and San Pellegrino. "I was on the other side of carbonation when carbonated soft drink consumers were looking for healthier alternatives, getting away from aspartame or high fructose corn syrup, and they moved over to Perrier, San Pellegrino, Polar, LaCroix," he said. "All of sparkling [water] exploded. We're seeing the same exact thing now, just the opposite." Hint's still flavored water offers "drinkability" and "pure hydration", giving the brand an edge over sparkling waters that cannot be drank as quickly, according to Pengue. He said it also has a "sensory softness" that appeals to consumers who do not like the bite of carbonation. Can-do attitude For decades, an aluminum can with a pull tab usually meant a carbonated beverage like beer, soda or seltzer was inside. But these days, most new non-carbonated drinks are coming in cans, resembling the seltzers and bubbly drinks from which they are stealing share. "The can is winning," Ball CEO Ronald Lewis said on the company's earnings conference call earlier this month. Liquid Death canned water drinks at a store in Pinole, California, US, on Monday, March 11, 2024. David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images He would know. Ball is the world's largest manufacturer of aluminum packaging. Celsius's Watson credits Liquid Death with paving the way for consumers to accept fizz-free canned drinks. When Liquid Death founder Mike Cessario started the company in 2017, he could not find a single bottler in the U.S. capable of putting still water in cans. Non-carbonated drinks require a quick dose of nitrogen to keep the can from collapsing on itself, presenting one issue for bottlers; carbonation creates high internal pressure to allows a can to keep its shape. Cessario told CNBC that the key to getting consumers to buy canned water - an otherwise unthinkable proposition - was by positioning Liquid Death as a cool brand. "We designed it to look more like a beer than a water, so it felt like something a lot more familiar to people than just like a weird bottled water in a can," Cessario said. Liquid Death has since launch sparkling and flavored sparkling lines, although it returned to its non-carbonated roots with iced tea in 2023. For beverage companies, aluminum cans are typically cheaper than glass bottles and a more sustainable option than plastic bottles. And for consumers, cans feel colder - and maybe even cooler, a callback to the last wave of trendy beverages during the seltzer boom.

title: Top Wall Street analysts like these dividend stocks for steady income
teaser: Analysts favor dividend stocks like Energy Transfer and Chevron amid market uncertainty, naming specific price targets and growth potential for investors.
summary: Amid market volatility from high Treasury yields and Middle East tensions, top Wall Street analysts are recommending three dividend stocks for steady income: Energy Transfer, Chevron, and Williams. Energy Transfer, which operates 140,000 miles of pipelines, raised its quarterly cash distribution to about 34 cents, leading TD Cowen to raise its price target to $23. For oil giant Chevron, which paid $6 billion to shareholders in Q1 2026, Wells Fargo reaffirmed a buy rating and a $222 price target. Lastly, Williams Companies, which offers a 53 cent dividend, is highlighted for its growing Power Innovation business. content: The stock market has been volatile due to rising Treasury yields and high oil prices amid tensions in the Middle East. Amid this uncertainty, dividend stocks can help investors secure consistent portfolio income. Top Wall Street analysts can inform investors on their search for attractive dividend stocks that have the ability to generate solid cash flows and pay dividends consistently. Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance. Energy Transfer Energy Transfer owns and operates a diversified portfolio of energy assets in the U.S., with about 140,000 miles of pipeline and associated infrastructure. The company recently announced an increase in its quarterly cash distribution to roughly 34 cents per common unit. Energy Transfer offers a yield of 6.7%. Recently, TD Cowen analyst Jason Gabelman reiterated a buy rating on Energy Transfer and slightly raised his price target to $23 from $22, saying, "We continue to see upside from underappreciated growth potential including underused assets in second-tier gas basins." The five-star analyst highlighted that Energy Transfer raised its full-year earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or EBITDA, guidance, with the company capturing its full-year optimization target in the first quarter itself. The revised outlook reflects upside from higher volumes, rates, and spreads. Gabelman expects EBITDA to reach the high end of the outlook at current commodity pricing. Furthermore, Gabelman expects ET to see a gain of $200 million in EBITDA from some new projects and 800 million cubic feet per day Haynesville volume growth this year, which is projected to add $100 million in EBITDA. Interestingly, the company expects to sanction multiple projects in 2026, which could contribute an additional $400 million in EBITDA. Gabelman ranks No. 660 among more than 12,200 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.4%. See Energy Transfer Financials on TipRanks. Chevron The next dividend-paying stock is oil-and-gas giant Chevron . The company recently announced its first-quarter results . It paid $6 billion of cash to shareholders in Q1 2026, including share repurchases of $2.5 billion and dividends of $3.5 billion. Chevron offers a current dividend yield of 3.7%. After hosting investor meetings with Chevron management, Wells Fargo analyst Sam Margolin reaffirmed a buy rating on CVX stock with a price target of $222 . "The company is in a favorable operating posture with transparent capital allocation and asset momentum yielding positive FCF/leverage outcomes," said the analyst. The five-star analyst noted Chevron's solid operating momentum, with key assets in the Permian, Kazakhstan, Australia LNG and Guyana running at full capacity or above their designed production levels. He added that CVX's downstream is gaining from stronger vertical integration and access to equity crude supplies in California and Asia, helping ease potential feedstock constraints. Additionally, Margolin highlighted that Chevron plans to maintain a 1 million barrels of oil equivalent per day plateau in the Permian Basin, driven by operational efficiencies achieved under its current program. He added that advanced chemicals treatment in wells, including both proprietary and third-party, has delivered about 20% productivity benefits in the first 10 months. The analyst also noted that CVX is advancing the first project under its power joint venture through an exclusivity agreement with Microsoft . Margolin believes that the company's advantage lies in being an early mover, with 5 gigawatts of turbines already on order, along with access to land and natural gas supply needed for power generation and data center development. Margolin ranks No. 455 among more than 12,200 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 71% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.3%.
